title: Me and You
description: Your first words out loud: who you are, where you are from, and the pronouns for pointing at yourself, the person in front of you and someone else. No verb 'to be' needed — Gulf Arabic just puts the pieces next to each other.
approach: GPA Phase 2 begins — first production. Pronouns are learned by pointing (at self, at the listener, at a photo), then the self-introduction is built up one chunk at a time and recorded.
unlock_condition: Record a three-line self-introduction (name, origin, student/job) that the speech check accepts, plus ≥9/12 on the pronoun tap quiz
can_do: Say who you are and where you are from
Point at yourself, the listener and a third person with the right pronoun

grammar.title: أنا، إنت، إنتي، هو، هي — who is who
grammar.explanation: Five words cover most of what you point at: أنا (I), إنت (you, to a man), إنتي (you, to a woman), هو (he) and هي (she). Gulf Arabic always tells the listener's gender, so there are two words for you — pick إنت or إنتي before you open your mouth. You will often hear أنا stretched to آنا; both are right. The pronoun usually comes first, and it is the only thing you need to start a sentence.

examples.arabic: هو من الرياض وهي من دبي
examples.transliteration: huwa min ir-riyaaḍ w-hiya min dubay
examples.english: He is from Riyadh and she is from Dubai

grammar.title: No word for 'is' — just put the pieces together
grammar.explanation: To say 'I am a student' you say the two words I and student: أنا طالب. There is no 'am', 'is' or 'are' in the present. The same works with a place (أنا من قطر), a name (هو أحمد) or a description (القهوة حارة). A question is the same sentence with your voice rising at the end — no extra word is added. This one habit unlocks hundreds of sentences with the words you already have.

examples.english: She is a student from Bahrain

culture.title: First names, and 'father of…'
culture.note: People use first names quickly, usually with a title in front: أستاذ for a man, أستاذة for a woman, or يا أخوي / يا أختي (brother / sister) between peers. Once a man has a son he is called أبو + the son's name — أبو محمد, shortened in the Gulf to بو محمد — and a woman أم محمد; friends may even invent a kunya for you before you have children. Expect to be called by your first name with أستاذ or مستر in front, and do not be surprised when the second question after your name is من وين؟ — where are you from.

phrases.english: My name is Sara, from London
Nice to meet you (we are honoured)

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first pronoun. Gulf speakers often lengthen it to آنا aana, and it is written both ways. It is all you need in front of a name, a nationality or a job — no 'am'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man pointing at his own chest with his thumb, plain background.
vocabulary.video_hint: Self-introductions at the start of vlogs and interviews: أنا + name.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Used only when speaking to a man or boy. You already heard it inside وإنت؟ in Lesson 2. Written إنت, انت or إنته; the final vowel is short and light.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman pointing with an open hand toward a man facing her, both in profile.
vocabulary.video_hint: Interviewers addressing a male guest; the وإنت؟ hand-back in greetings.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The feminine you. The only difference from إنت is the final -i, but the difference is not optional — using إنت to a woman sounds like a mistake, not a simplification. Kuwait and the Emirates sometimes write it إنتِ with a kasra.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man pointing with an open hand toward a woman in an abaya facing him, both in profile.
vocabulary.video_hint: Anyone addressing a woman on camera; family vlogs where a husband speaks to his wife.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Pronounced huwa, often shortened to hu in fast speech. Also used for 'it' when the thing is masculine (most words without ة). Point at a photo of a man to make it stick.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two people looking at a framed photo of a man on a table; one points at the photo.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone introducing a third person on camera: هذا … هو …

vocabulary.teaching_note: Pronounced hiya, often just hi. Also 'it' for feminine things (words ending in ة like سيارة, قهوة). Notice هو and هي differ only in the final vowel, exactly like إنت and إنتي.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two people looking at a framed photo of a woman; one points at the photo.
vocabulary.video_hint: Introducing a female relative or friend; describing a woman who is not present.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The base word. In Gulf speech a helping vowel breaks the cluster, so it sounds like isim. You will meet it almost only with an ending attached — اسمي, اسمك — which is why the next two cards exist.
vocabulary.image_scene: A blank name badge on a lanyard, the line for the name empty.
vocabulary.video_hint: Baby-naming discussions in family vlogs; a name written on a form or cup.

vocabulary.teaching_note: اسم + the ending -i (my). No verb needed: اسمي سارة is the whole sentence. This is your first taste of the possessive endings that Lesson 5 explains properly.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman holding up a name badge that reads a clear first name, pointing at it.

example.english: My name is Khalid — and you?

vocabulary.video_hint: The first sentence of most self-introductions.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The what-word شـ fused onto اسمك (your name) — one quick word: shismak. To a woman: شسمج shismich in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Emirates, شسمك shismik in Saudi. Riyadh also says وش اسمك, Jeddah إيش اسمك, Dubai شو اسمك. All are the same question.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man at a reception desk leaning forward with a questioning look at a visitor.
vocabulary.video_hint: Street interviews and children being asked their names; the very first question.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Short, unstressed, glued to the next word: min il-kuwayt. It also means 'from' in time and 'of' in quantities later on, but for now it introduces where you are from.
vocabulary.image_scene: A map of the Gulf with an arrow pointing out from one city toward the viewer.
vocabulary.video_hint: Origin questions and answers in interviews; travel vlogs saying where a dish or a guest is from.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Say it as one breath and add your country or city: أنا من لندن, أنا من أمريكا. Cities take the article when they have one in Arabic (الرياض, الدوحة, الكويت); Dubai, Jeddah and most foreign cities do not.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young woman pointing at her own country on a world map, smiling at the camera.

example.english: I am from Kuwait — and you (f)?

vocabulary.video_hint: Guests introducing themselves on talk shows; vloggers stating their city.

vocabulary.english: nice to meet you (we are honoured)
vocabulary.teaching_note: Said once names are exchanged. The reply is الشرف لي (the honour is mine) or simply تشرفنا back. Younger speakers also say فرصة سعيدة. Note the sh sound leading straight into a doubled r.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two men shaking hands after an introduction, both smiling, a third person looking on.

example.english: I am Sara — nice to meet you

vocabulary.video_hint: The closing beat of introductions on talk shows and first meetings in dramas.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first job word, chosen because so many learners are one. A woman is طالبة ṭaalba; the plural is طلاب. Starts with the emphatic ط you heard in طيب.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man with a backpack and a notebook outside a university gate.

example.english: I am a student at Kuwait University

vocabulary.video_hint: University day-in-the-life vlogs; people stating what they do in interviews.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The nationality pattern: country + -i. Feminine adds ة: سعودية. The same ending gives كويتي, قطري, بحريني, إماراتي and بريطاني — learn one and you can recognise them all.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man in a red-and-white shemagh and white thobe standing in front of a green flag.
vocabulary.video_hint: People stating nationality in interviews; national-day content.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.english: Peace be upon you — I am Sara

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.arabic: وعليكم السلام، هلا سارة. أنا خالد
dialogue.transliteration: w-ʿalaykum is-salaam, hala saara. ana khaalid
dialogue.english: And upon you peace, hi Sara. I am Khalid

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.english: Nice to meet you. Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.english: I am from Riyadh. And you?

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.english: I am from London. I am a student

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.english: How nice. And him — what's his name?

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.english: He is Ahmed, a student too

sound_spotlight.explanation: The glottal catch at the start of أنا and اسم is barely there in Gulf speech; أنا often opens on a long aa, and اسمي runs straight on from the word before it. Expect words to begin more softly than the spelling suggests.
The same ending you met in شلونك: -ak to a man, and to a woman -ik in Saudi or -ich in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Emirates. Now you produce it: choose before you speak.
No question word is added for yes-no questions; only the melody changes. Say the statement, then let the last syllable climb. Record it and compare with the native line.

lesson_sequence.detail: A university courtyard, two students meeting. One line of English: today you say who you are. Tap يلّا.

Five pronoun cards: the illustration shows who is pointed at; audio plays; the learner repeats and taps the matching figure in a three-person scene (me / you / that person). Gender of 'you' is drilled with paired photos.
Three chunks appear in order — اسمي …, أنا من …, أنا طالب/طالبة — each heard, then the learner picks their own name, city and role from a small menu and hears the line assembled.
The learner records the three-line introduction; the speech check compares against the native line and marks the pronoun/gender ending.
شسمك؟ and من وين؟ are drilled as the hand-back: a native asks, the learner answers, then the learner asks the native (record-and-compare).
The seven-line dialogue plays; on the second pass the learner takes Sara's lines.
Twelve items: pronoun tap (hear هو/هي/إنت/إنتي, tap the figure) and gap-fill for the phrases. Counter rolls to 52. Nudge: introduce yourself to someone in Arabic this week.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Introduce yourself to one Arabic speaker this week: اسمي …، أنا من …. Then ask شسمك؟ and listen for the answer.
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. The first real production task; the guaranteed follow-up question is من وين.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Look at a group photo. Say هو or هي for each person, out loud, quickly.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. Drills he/she without needing a partner.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tell your tutor: ask me my name and where I am from, then ask me about two people in a photo.
real_world_prompts.context: Before a tutor session. Runs the whole lesson as a here-and-now game.

video_needs.scene: A self-introduction on camera: name, city, what they do. Street interviews asking name and origin, and talk-show guests introducing themselves are ideal; the pronoun should be audible at the start of the line.
